articles.title: Planning Permission Granted for Seven Homes on Former New Jerusalem Church Site in Middleton
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has approved plans for seven new family homes on the site of the former New Jerusalem Church on Egerton Street, Middleton, despite objections regarding parking and green space.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has granted planning permission for the construction of seven new homes on the site of the former New Jerusalem Church, located on Egerton Street in Middleton. The church, which was established before 1886, was demolished in 2012, leaving the site vacant.

The developer, Zest Eco, proposed the construction of seven three-bedroom townhouses, each featuring private gardens and dedicated parking. The planning documents state that the development aims to meet the identified need for family housing rather than higher-density flat accommodation. The new homes will include rear dormers and solar panels, with access provided via a new dropped kerb from Egerton Street.

Despite the approval, the plans faced five objections from local residents. Concerns included the potential loss of on-street parking for existing residents, fears of overdevelopment, and the loss of green space in the area. The council's planning committee noted these objections but ultimately decided to proceed with the development, citing the benefits of regenerating a brownfield site and providing much-needed family housing.

The development is expected to contribute positively to the local community by enhancing the residential character of the neighbourhood. Construction is likely to commence in the near future, although specific timelines have yet to be confirmed. Residents will be informed of any significant developments regarding the project as it progresses.

articles.title: Rochdale & District Camera Club Welcomes New Members to Weekly Meetings
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale & District Camera Club invites photography enthusiasts to join its weekly meetings at Syke Community Base, offering a variety of activities for all skill levels.
articles.content_html:
Photography enthusiasts in Rochdale have a wealth of opportunities to explore their passion through local camera clubs. The Rochdale & District Camera Club, which meets every Tuesday evening at Syke Community Base & Methodist Chapel, is one such group welcoming new members. The club aims to foster a friendly environment where photographers of all skill levels can come together to enjoy photography, learn from one another, and enhance their skills.

The club's programme includes a mix of visiting speakers, practical sessions, competitions, and members' presentations. Recent activities have covered a range of topics, from portraiture and image editing to creative challenges like light painting. The club encourages members to take their cameras outdoors, promoting the idea that photography is best enjoyed in the field.

Martyn Slater, a member of the club, highlighted the diverse photographic subjects available in the area, including wildlife, landscapes, and architecture. He noted that the club's activities are designed to inspire creativity and provide practical experience, making it an ideal place for both novice and experienced photographers.

For those interested in joining, the Rochdale & District Camera Club offers a warm welcome to anyone looking to improve their photography skills or simply enjoy the art of capturing images. More information can be found on their website or by attending a meeting.

articles.title: Why Rochdale says “cruckle”
articles.excerpt: How a short, local verb — to “cruckle” your ankle — links Rochdale speech to an older northern‑English dialect family and why locals still claim it as their own.
articles.summary: How a short, local verb — to “cruckle” your ankle — links Rochdale speech to an older northern‑English dialect family and why locals still claim it as their own.
articles.body:
If you grew up in parts of Rochdale you’ll recognise the line: “I cruckled me ankle.” Locally, to “cruckle” means to roll, twist or go over on your ankle — that sharp, hobbling stumble you can sometimes walk off but that still makes you wince.

That everyday meaning is not just neighbourhood folklore. A recent perceptual‑dialect study of Greater Manchester (draw‑a‑map / keywords method) collected hundreds of free comments from residents and found “cruckle” listed among the words people explicitly associate with Rochdale speech, alongside other locally salient terms such as guinnel (ginnel) and “broad.” In other words, people across the region perceive cruckle as a recognisable Rochdale marker rather than as a random slang item.

But cruckle is not a brand‑new invention restricted to a single street. Historical dialect scholarship records older and related forms — most commonly crookle — with senses that cover bending, making crooked, stooping or hobbling. Joseph Wright’s English Dialect Dictionary (late 19th/early 20th century) collects crookle and similar headwords from northern and midland counties in senses that naturally extend to limping or going wrong with a foot. Those historical attestations show the word belongs to a wider northern‑English dialect family rather than springing up overnight in Rochdale.

The wider picture is supported by Scots and northern dialect material. The Dictionaries of the Scots Language records cognate variants (kruggle, cruggle, cruckle, krukel) with meanings such as to crouch, huddle or bend; the entry brings together quotations dating from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. These cognates point to a common root (crook/krug‑) and the frequentative/imitative suffix ‑le that turns roots into verbs meaning repeated or small actions (so crook → crookle/cruckle).

So why does Rochdale feel particularly identified with the term? Two complementary facts explain it. First, ordinary use: people in and around Rochdale still use cruckle in the ankle‑sense, keeping the word alive in everyday speech. Second, folk‑awareness: perceptual research shows locals and neighbouring Greater Manchester residents explicitly list cruckle when asked to name words that signal Rochdale speech. That combination — continued usage plus shared recognition — is what gives the word its local badge value.

Is cruckle unique to Rochdale? Strictly speaking no. Dialect records show related forms across northern England and in Scots dialects, so the root and pattern are regional. But uniqueness in dialects is often a matter of degree. Many neighbouring places will have similar old verbs or different local favourites; what sets Rochdale’s claim apart is the particular survival and social visibility of cruckle there. In short: the etymological family is wider, but the modern reputation and everyday ankle‑sense are strongly tied to Rochdale in people’s minds.

Why does this matter beyond trivia? Small, everyday words such as cruckle are useful signals for dialect researchers because they reveal both living speech practice (who says what, where) and folk perception (which words people think define a place). Contemporary perceptual methods — asking residents to draw or list the words they associate with local speech — combine with archival lexicography to show how old dialect vocabulary is kept alive (or lost) and how language becomes a local identity marker.

If you’re from Rochdale, cruckle is one of those short pieces of speech that can prompt a knowing nod; if you’re visiting, try it after a tumble in a ginnel and you’ll soon find out whether you’ve landed in the right place. For readers who want to check the research behind this piece, the perceptual study and the historical dictionary records are publicly accessible and show both the modern association with Rochdale and the word’s wider dialect history.

articles.title: Bonfire Night Event Scheduled for Bowlee Community Park in Middleton on November 2
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council will host a Bonfire Night event at Bowlee Community Park on November 2, featuring fireworks and a family funfair, as part of a series of celebrations across the borough.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council is set to host its first Bonfire Night event in Middleton on Monday, November 2, 2026. The celebration will take place at Bowlee Community Park and will feature a fireworks display alongside a family funfair, providing entertainment for local residents.

This event is part of a wider series of Bonfire Night celebrations across the borough, which will also include fireworks displays in Rochdale and Heywood. The festivities aim to bring communities together and offer a safe environment for families to enjoy the evening.

In addition to the Middleton event, Manchester City Council has announced the return of fireworks to Heaton Park for the first time in seven years. The council will hold two displays on Saturday, November 7, 2026, including a reduced-noise display at 5pm for families and SEND audiences, followed by the main display at 8pm.

Councillor Garry Bridges, Leader of Manchester City Council, emphasised the importance of community events, stating that they help bridge cultural divides and create shared experiences. The decision to exclude bonfires this year aims to focus on family-friendly fireworks, ensuring a safe and enjoyable atmosphere for all attendees.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The rocky cleft known as the Fairies’ Chapel is a real landscape feature with a long history of local storytelling — but the supernatural claims rest in folklore, not in official records.
articles.summary: The rocky cleft known as the Fairies’ Chapel is a real landscape feature with a long history of local storytelling — but the supernatural claims rest in folklore, not in official records.
articles.body:
Healey Dell sits where the River Spodden squeezes through a narrow gorge known locally as the Thrutch, a shady, waterfall‑scattered hollow two miles north of Rochdale town centre. Today it is a council‑managed nature reserve with a heritage centre, tea rooms and family trails; the long stone viaduct that towers above the gorge is a Grade II listed structure and the Dell is promoted as a place of industrial archaeology and wild beauty. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

The name “Fairies’ Chapel” points to one of the Dell’s most persistent stories: a pocket of hollowed rock that, to Victorian and earlier visitors, looked like a tiny church with a pulpit and seats carved by the water. Local guidebooks and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre explain that the “chapel” is essentially a water‑worn niche in the rock — a natural feature shaped by erosion rather than human carving. That explanation sits alongside the telling that a great summer storm in the 1830s changed the Spodden’s course and altered or buried parts of the formation people once pointed to. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

Where the written history stops, folklore gathers. The most often‑repeated version appears in nineteenth‑century collections of Lancashire tales: the Fairies’ Chapel becomes the stage for tricks, warnings and moral tales involving fairies, witches, prophetic “Fairy Queens” and local characters such as millers and gentry. Robert Roby’s Lancashire Legends (a Victorian compilation that survives in full online) gives a long, theatrical account in which a narrow rocky hollow is haunted by “the good people,” encounters with enchanted hares and strange lights, and episodes of bewitchment and retribution. These are literary and oral traditions rather than records of events that can be checked against archives. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c1/Lancashire_legends_%28IA_lancashirelegend00roby%29.pdf))

Later local retellings and the Dell’s own heritage material mix Roby’s account with other regional motifs: witches turned to stone by a Fairy King, a fortune‑teller called Mother Bagden, and love stories involving the Byron and Chadwick families. These stories are clearly labelled as legend by the heritage centre and by council information aimed at visitors; they help explain why the spot became one of the Dell’s most evocative attractions, but they are not supported by contemporary documentary evidence of supernatural events. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

That distinction matters. The documented facts are straightforward: Healey Dell is an historically important landscape (with a listed viaduct and remnants of mills) and it is managed as a local nature reserve. The physical rock features people called the Fairies’ Chapel are the result of ordinary geological and fluvial action; floods and industrial change have altered the appearance of the Dell since at least the early nineteenth century. Claims that fairies, witches or a Fairy King literally created or inhabit the chapel are part of oral tradition and folklore — rich, culturally valuable stories, but not verifiable historical fact. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

If you come looking for fairies, the sensible local advice is to bring imagination and respect. The Dell’s folklore is part of what makes it special: the stories connect people across generations to place and to the Dell’s industrial and natural past. If you want the clearest separation between what’s recorded and what’s told, read the nineteenth‑century legends as folklore, and the council and heritage centre material as the place’s recorded history and practical visitor information. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c1/Lancashire_legends_%28IA_lancashirelegend00roby%29.pdf))

Bottom line: there is nothing in the official record to confirm supernatural activity at the Fairies’ Chapel — only enduring, well‑documented local stories that have been collected, retold and celebrated by authors and by the Healey Dell community. The chapel is best enjoyed as a meeting point of geology, industrial archaeology and imagination — a small landscape where the boundary between history and legend is part of the attraction. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

articles.title: Rochdale AFC Secures 2-0 Victory Over Oldham Athletic
articles.excerpt: Rochdale AFC moved off the bottom of the League Two table with a 2-0 win against Oldham Athletic in a closely contested Greater Manchester derby on Saturday, September 19, 2026.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC lifted themselves off the foot of the League Two table with a decisive 2-0 victory against Oldham Athletic in their Greater Manchester derby on Saturday, September 19, 2026. The match took place at the Crown Oil Arena, where the home side made a strong start, taking the lead just seven minutes into the game.

The opening goal came from Dan Moss, who capitalised on a low delivery from Charlie Tasker, combining well with Jonny Smith down the right flank. Moss swept the ball into the roof of the net, giving Rochdale an early advantage. Oldham's Mike Fondop had a chance to equalise shortly after, but he missed an open goal, sliding the ball wide of the post after a mistake from Rochdale goalkeeper Nils Ramming.

As the match progressed, Oldham continued to press for an equaliser, with Kane Drummond's delivery across the face of goal eluding both Fondop and substitute Calum Kavanagh. However, it was Rochdale who struck again on 62 minutes, doubling their lead. A kick from Oldham's keeper Matt Hudson was met by Baba Adeeko, who headed the ball forward for Dajaune Brown. Brown advanced into the penalty area, sidestepped defender Donervon Daniels, and fired a powerful shot into the bottom corner.

This victory not only boosts Rochdale's position in the league but also provides a much-needed morale lift as they aim to improve their performance in the ongoing season. The team will look to build on this success in their upcoming fixtures as they strive to move further away from the relegation zone.

The Heywood Community Gala, which took place from 18 to 20 September at The Pig and Whistle, has come under scrutiny after photos from the event showed a significantly smaller setup than the colourful promotional material suggested. The event was advertised as featuring large fairground rides, live music, street food, and children's entertainment, but images released on Saturday morning depicted only a handful of gazebos outside the venue, with no large rides in sight.

The promotional artwork, generated by AI, depicted a vibrant scene with performers, balloons, and crowds, leading to comparisons on social media with Glasgow's infamous Willy Wonka experience, which faced similar criticism in 2024 for not meeting expectations. A Facebook page, Cameron Boland - Scam Event Watch & Awareness, has been vocal in its criticism of the Heywood event, alleging it was a scam and questioning the adequacy of security and entertainment arrangements.

Cameron Boland, the organiser, has been accused of mismanaging previous events, including a similar gala that was cancelled by Salford City Council and Greater Manchester Police in August. While the Facebook page has raised concerns about the gala's setup, including claims that performers were situated on a rug between tables, these allegations have not been independently verified. The photographs from the event do show activity taking place, but they do not provide a complete picture of what was available throughout the three-day event.

Kelly, the tenant and operator of The Pig and Whistle, defended the event, stating that it was still ongoing and that there were activities planned for the remainder of the weekend. The situation has raised questions about the expectations set by promotional materials versus the actual experience provided, highlighting the importance of transparency in event advertising.
